claim: Across diverse microbiotas, species abundances vary in time with distinctive statistical behaviors that appear to generalize across hosts.
source: Across diverse microbiotas, species abundances vary in time with distinctive statistical behaviors that appear to generalize across hosts, but the origins and implications of these patterns remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation about microbiotas.

claim: Many macroecological patterns can be quantitatively recapitulated by a simple class of consumer-resource models in which metabolic capabilities are randomly drawn from a common statistical distribution.
source: Here, we show that many of these macroecological patterns can be quantitatively recapitulated by a simple class of consumer-resource models, in which the metabolic capabilities of different species are randomly drawn from a common statistical distribution.
evidence: This is the main finding presented in the abstract and demonstrated throughout the manuscript with simulations and data comparisons.

claim: The consumer-resource model parametrizes community properties using only a small number of global parameters including total number of resources, typical resource fluctuations over time, and average overlap in resource-consumption profiles.
source: Our model parametrizes the consumer-resource properties of a community using only a small number of global parameters, including the total number of resources, typical resource fluctuations over time, and the average overlap in resource-consumption profiles across species.
evidence: This describes the model structure presented in the abstract and detailed in the Results section.

claim: Variation in macroscopic parameters strongly affects the time series statistics generated by the model.
source: We show that variation in these macroscopic parameters strongly affects the time series statistics generated by the model, and we identify specific sets of global parameters that can recapitulate macroecological patterns across wide-ranging microbiotas, including the human gut, saliva, and vagina, as well as mouse gut and rice, without needing to specify microscopic details of resource consumption.
evidence: This is demonstrated through systematic parameter space exploration shown in Figure 3.

claim: Specific sets of global parameters can recapitulate macroecological patterns across human gut, saliva, vagina, mouse gut, and rice microbiotas without specifying microscopic details of resource consumption.
source: We show that variation in these macroscopic parameters strongly affects the time series statistics generated by the model, and we identify specific sets of global parameters that can recapitulate macroecological patterns across wide-ranging microbiotas, including the human gut, saliva, and vagina, as well as mouse gut and rice, without needing to specify microscopic details of resource consumption.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplements 1–6 showing fits to multiple microbiota datasets.

claim: Resource competition may be a dominant driver of community dynamics.
source: These findings suggest that resource competition may be a dominant driver of community dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the success of the consumer-resource model in recapitulating experimental data.

claim: Consumer-resource models capture a core set of interactions among community members based on their competition for nutrients.
source: CR models capture a core set of interactions among members of a community based on their competition for nutrients, and have demonstrated the capacity to recapitulate important properties of microbial communities such as diversity and stability (Niehaus et al., 2019; Posfai et al., 2017; Tikhonov and Monasson, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on consumer-resource models.

claim: Consumer-resource models have demonstrated the capacity to recapitulate important properties of microbial communities such as diversity and stability.
source: CR models capture a core set of interactions among members of a community based on their competition for nutrients, and have demonstrated the capacity to recapitulate important properties of microbial communities such as diversity and stability (Niehaus et al., 2019; Posfai et al., 2017; Tikhonov and Monasson, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It remains challenging to determine all parameters for a community of native complexity from the bottom-up.
source: However, while model parameters such as resource consumption rates are beginning to be uncovered in the context of in vitro experiments (Goldford et al., 2018; Hart et al., 2019; Liao et al., 2020), it remains challenging to determine all parameters for a community of native complexity from the bottom-up.
evidence: This is stated as a known challenge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Species abundances fluctuate around stable, host-specific values in healthy humans.
source: Analyses of longitudinal data have shown that species abundances fluctuate around stable, host-specific values in healthy humans (Caporaso et al., 2011; David et al., 2014; Faith et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous longitudinal studies.

claim: In human and mouse gut microbiotas, the temporal variance of different species scales as a power of their mean abundance (Taylor's law).
source: For example, in human and mouse gut microbiotas, the temporal variance of different species scales as a power of their mean abundance ('Taylor's law', Taylor, 1961) and deviations from this trend can highlight species that are transient invaders (Ji et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Taylor's original work and recent applications.

claim: Deviations from Taylor's law can highlight species that are transient invaders.
source: For example, in human and mouse gut microbiotas, the temporal variance of different species scales as a power of their mean abundance ('Taylor's law', Taylor, 1961) and deviations from this trend can highlight species that are transient invaders (Ji et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ji et al., 2020.

claim: The relative contributions of intrinsic versus environmental processes can be distinguished using autoregressive models.
source: For example, the relative contributions of intrinsic versus environmental processes can be distinguished using autoregressive models whose output values depend linearly on values at previous times and external noise (Gibbons et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gibbons et al., 2017.

claim: Resources in the model are defined at a coarse-grained level such that individual resources represent effective groups of metabolites or niches.
source: The resources in this model are defined at a coarse-grained level, such that individual resources represent effective groups of metabolites or niches.
evidence: This describes the conceptual interpretation of resources in the model.

claim: The model was simulated using a serial dilution scheme to mimic the punctuated turnover of gut microbiotas due to multiple feedings and defecations between sampling times.
source: We simulated the dynamics in Equation 1 using a serial dilution scheme (Erez et al., 2020) to mimic the punctuated turnover of gut microbiotas due to multiple feedings and defecations between sampling times.
evidence: This describes the simulation approach, with citation to Erez et al., 2020.

claim: The family level is an appropriate coarse graining of metabolic capabilities.
source: Previous studies have suggested that the family level is an appropriate coarse graining of metabolic capabilities (Goldford et al., 2018; Louca et al., 2016; Tian et al., 2020), thus we assumed, unless otherwise specified, that each consumer grouping i within our model represents a taxonomic family, and combined abundances of empirical operational taxonomic units (OTUs) or amplicon sequencing variants (ASVs; Callahan et al., 2016) at the family level for analyses (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Only taxa with relative abundance >10^-4 at any given time point were examined due to typical limits of detection of 16S amplicon sequencing.
source: Given the typical limits of detection of 16S amplicon sequencing data sets, we only examined time series statistics for taxa with relative abundance >10–4 at any given time point.
evidence: This describes a methodological constraint based on sequencing limitations.

claim: Random realizations of the model generated similar time series statistics, whose typical behavior strongly varied with the global parameters.
source: As expected, we found that random realizations of our model (i.e., different resource consumption matrices drawn from the same ensemble) generated similar time series statistics, whose typical behavior strongly varied with the global parameters of the model.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulations.

claim: Only small subsets of the parameters led to time series statistics that agreed with experiments.
source: In particular, only small subsets of the parameters led to time series statistics that agreed with experiments, as we show below.
evidence: This is demonstrated through parameter space exploration and fitting to data.

claim: A specific combination of parameters was identified that could reproduce all statistical behaviors of human gut microbiota within the consumer-resource model.
source: Through an exhaustive search of parameter space, we identified a specific combination of parameters that could reproduce all of these behaviors within our simple CR model (Figure 2F, G and K).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2F, G, and K showing model fits to data.

claim: The model was able to simultaneously capture at least eight statistical behaviors in a microbiota time series with only four parameters.
source: Therefore, our model was able to simultaneously capture at least eight statistical behaviors in a microbiota time series with only four parameters, each of which may represent biologically relevant features of the community.
evidence: This summarizes the model's performance as demonstrated in Figure 2.

claim: The modeling framework was able to quantitatively recapitulate almost all statistics at both genus and class taxonomic levels.
source: To determine whether our model can be used to analyze time series statistics at other taxonomic levels, we analyzed the same data set (Caporaso et al., 2011) at finer (genus) and coarser (class) taxonomic levels, both of which exhibited qualitatively similar statistical behaviors as the family level. Our modeling framework was able to quantitatively recapitulate almost all statistics at both levels (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The Bacteroides genus dominated the observed rank abundance distribution at the genus level, while the CR model predicted a more even distribution.
source: A notable exception is that the Bacteroides genus dominated the observed rank abundance distribution at the genus level, while our CR model predicted a more even distribution (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 as a discrepancy between model and data.

claim: Simulations of a no-competition model confirmed the β scalings in the high sparsity limits.
source: Simulations of a no-competition model in which consumers consume distinct sets of resources confirmed the scalings in these limits (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: External fluctuations in resource levels may be responsible for generating species abundance variations, while intrinsic properties of resource competition can determine the resulting scaling exponents of many statistical behaviors.
source: Thus, our results suggest that while external fluctuations in resource levels may be responsible for generating species abundance variations, the intrinsic properties of resource competition can determine the resulting scaling exponents of many statistical behaviors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analysis of shuffled versus original time series.

claim: The measured distribution of pairwise correlations between consumer abundances is much broader than the prediction of a non-interacting model.
source: We reasoned that the discrepancies between experimental data and the null model could be due to the lack of interspecies interactions. To test this hypothesis, we examined the pairwise correlations between the consumer abundances across sampling times. The measured distribution of pairwise correlations is much broader than the prediction of the non-interacting model, which is sharply peaked about zero as expected (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4 comparing data to null model predictions.

claim: The distribution of correlations predicted by the CR model was in much closer agreement with experimental data than the non-interacting model.
source: By contrast, the distribution of correlations predicted by our CR model without any additional fitting was in much closer agreement with the experimental data (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4.

claim: Interspecies interactions are required to capture important details of community dynamics.
source: These findings imply that interspecies interactions are required to capture important details of community dynamics.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of models with and without interactions.

claim: The results are robust to assumptions regarding metabolic trade-offs and saturation kinetics.
source: This suggests that our results are robust to assumptions regarding metabolic trade-offs and saturation kinetics.
evidence: This is inferred from the analyses in Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: While pairwise interactions between taxa are likely sufficient to recapitulate experimental data, their parameters must be drawn from particular ensembles that can be more simply described in the CR framework.
source: Together, these results suggest that while pairwise interactions between taxa are likely sufficient to recapitulate the experimental data, their parameters must be drawn from particular ensembles that can be more simply described in the CR framework.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing CR-converted and random gLV models in Figure 4—figure supplements 4 and 5.

claim: The CR model successfully reproduced experimental statistics across all communities including human gut, saliva, vagina, mouse gut, and rice.
source: In addition to microbiotas from the human and mouse gut (Caporaso et al., 2011; Carmody et al., 2015; David et al., 2014), we examined communities from the human vagina (Song et al., 2020), human saliva (David et al., 2014), and in and around rice roots (Edwards et al., 2018). The time series statistics of these microbiotas varied broadly (Figure 5A). Nevertheless, our model successfully reproduced the experimental statistics across all communities (Figure 5—figure supplements 1–6), suggesting that simple CR models can capture many of the macroscopic features of these microbiotas.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplements 1–6.

claim: Metabolic capability is a major determinant of community composition.
source: The success of our CR model in reproducing experimental time series statistics is consistent with bioinformatics-guided analyses of complex communities demonstrating that metabolic capability is a major determinant of community composition (Louca et al., 2016; Tian et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous bioinformatics studies.

claim: The contributions of a reservoir of species or other forms of species re-introduction are important for the dynamics of wide-ranging microbiotas.
source: Our results also suggest that the contributions of a reservoir of species or other forms of species re-introduction are important for the dynamics of wide-ranging microbiotas.
evidence: This is inferred from the model's dependence on reservoir assumptions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The existence of a reservoir is consistent with previous experimental work in mice.
source: The existence of a reservoir is consistent with previous experimental work in mice (Ng et al., 2019), but further work is required to investigate how species re-introduction occurs in other systems.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ng et al., 2019.
